content: The subcutaneous tissue, also known as the subcutis, is the layer of tissue located directly beneath the cutis (the skin). This layer is primarily composed of adipose tissue, which serves several physiological purposes, including providing insulation to regulate body temperature and acting as a reservoir for nutrient storage. Subcutaneous injections involve the administration of a fluid or a solid pellet directly into the subcutis. This method is commonly employed for delivering various medical treatments. For instance, subcutaneous fluid injections are used to administer vaccines and medications. In some cases, a solid pellet may be injected into the subcutaneous tissue to provide a sustained release of medication over an extended period. An example of this is the administration of goserelin, a medication delivered via a subcutaneous pellet. The subcutaneous route of injection is advantageous because it allows for slow and consistent absorption of the administered substance. This makes it one of the preferred parenteral (non-oral) methods of drug delivery. For example, a 10.8 mg implant syringe is specifically designed for subcutaneous use. After the injection of such an implant, the typical injection site may show visible signs, such as an entry wound and a bruise caused by the ejection of the pellet.
